name: Proportion dominance
statement: People value a fixed saving more when it is a larger share of the group at risk, and some will take the larger share even when it saves fewer lives.
meaning: The claim is about the denominator. Saving 4,500 refugees is the same saving whether the camp holds 11,000 people or 250,000, and the number rescued is what a life-saving budget buys. People rate the first as the better use of the aid. The weak form of the claim is a framing effect: a fixed benefit is judged larger against a smaller background. The strong form is a preference reversal that costs lives, where someone shown both options picks 225 of 300 over 230 of 920. Only the strong form conflicts with the arithmetic, and it is the rarer of the two. The idea travels under several names. Jenni and Loewenstein called it the reference group effect, Fetherstonhaugh and colleagues called it psychophysical numbing, and Bartels credits the label used here to Finucane, Peters and Slovic.

origin.who: David Fetherstonhaugh, Paul Slovic, Stephen M. Johnson and James Friedrich
origin.note: Volume 14 issue 3 carried three papers on the same pattern: Fetherstonhaugh and colleagues at pages 283 to 300, Baron at 301 to 309, and Jenni and Loewenstein on the identifiable victim effect. Baron's own paper says his results are consistent with the other two and argues for a different reading of them, a general confusion of proportions with differences rather than a psychophysical value function. The name proportion dominance came later.

evidence: Fetherstonhaugh and colleagues ran three studies. In Study 1, 54 undergraduate volunteers compared government programmes in pairs, two domestic and two supplying clean water to Rwandan refugee camps of 11,000 and 250,000 people. Both camp programmes were stated to save 4,500 lives. The small camp was preferred, F(1, 52) = 8.24, p < .01, with mean preference 0.45 against -0.20. In Study 2, 133 respondents rated the benefit of sending a water-purifying plane. Benefit was rated 6.46 for the small camp and 4.54 for the large one, F(1, 132) = 160.5, p < .001. Study 2 also found respondents rated the plane more beneficial when the camp already had most of its water need met, F(1, 132) = 15.35, p < .001. Study 3 paid 165 Oregon students to say how many lives a treatment must save to merit $10 million. Asked one disease at a time, 65% raised their threshold as the disease grew, with median demands of 9,000, 60,000 and 100,000 lives for diseases killing 15,000, 160,000 and 290,000 a year. Shown all three side by side with the lives each treatment saved, 60% ranked by lives saved and 16% by proportion. Baron put willingness to pay on the same question. His 95 respondents gave geometric mean payments of $143 to cure 900 people and $74 to cure 90, and $129 when the cure rate was .90 against $89 when it was .09, t = 5.29, p < .0005. The two effects correlated negatively across subjects, r = -.22, p = .031, so people divide into those watching the number and those watching the ratio. In his second experiment, 29 respondents allocated a hypothetical budget across 18 causes of death, once for a 5% cut and once for a cut of 2,600 lives. The median within-subject correlation between the two allocations was .80, and 26% of respondents gave answers correlating at 1.00. Bartels forced the tradeoff. Across his first three studies participants chose between saving 225 of 300 and 230 of 920. With 44 Northwestern undergraduates rating one option at a time, willingness to support ran at .88 for the small reference group and .76 for the large, t(43) = 4.85, p < .001, eta squared .353. Shown both options together, 48% of responses fell on the half of the scale favouring the smaller reference group. Asked afterwards which attribute should count, 70 participants rated the absolute difference more important than the relative one, .74 against .52, t(69) = 4.39, p < .001. Study 4 dropped human lives entirely and asked 168 participants to set a rebate that would make a discount on a $100 jacket as attractive as $10 off a $20 calculator. Responses shifted with which item carried the unknown on all three such items, smallest chi-squared(2) = 12.25, p = .002.

replication.headline: Five preregistered replications on 4,799 people split down the middle: the benefit-rating study reproduced at partial eta squared 0.62, and the programme-choice study reversed three times.
replication.detail: Ziano and eleven colleagues ran direct replications of Fetherstonhaugh's Studies 1 and 2 on MTurk and Prolific, total N = 4,799, all preregistered. Study 2 held. The camp-size effect on benefit ratings came out at partial eta squared 0.62, 90% CI 0.58 to 0.66 on 499 participants, and 0.24, 90% CI 0.21 to 0.27 in a second collection, against the original 0.55, 90% CI 0.45 to 0.62. Study 1 did not hold, and it did not merely fail. All three attempts found the effect running the other way, with participants preferring aid to the larger camp: 0.06, 90% CI 0.02 to 0.10 on 386 MTurk participants, 0.21, 90% CI 0.17 to 0.26 on British participants, and 0.13, 90% CI 0.08 to 0.17 when the two camp programmes were compared head to head. The original Study 1 effect was 0.14, 90% CI 0.02 to 0.28. The authors name the reversal psychophysical sensitization and suggest people read a bigger camp as a worse emergency. The structured figures below report the original Study 2 against the first Study 2 replication only, because a single pair cannot carry a result that points both ways. The strong form of the claim has held up better than Study 1 did. Mata gave the tradeoff to 100 Portuguese psychology undergraduates and 104 MTurk workers, and found 35% and 52% of choices taking the higher proportion when it meant saving fewer lives. Those same participants scored lower on the Cognitive Reflection Test, r = -.26, p = .008, and on a numeracy scale, r = -.20, p = .047, and answered faster.

study.cite: Ziano, I., Xiao, Q., Yeung, S. K., Wong, C. Y., Cheung, M. Y., Lo, C. Y., Yan, H. C., Narendra, G. I., Kwan, L. W., Chow, C. S., Man, C. Y., & Feldman, G. (2021). Numbing or sensitization? Replications and extensions of Fetherstonhaugh et al. (1997)'s "Insensitivity to the Value of Human Life". Journal of Experimental Social Psychology, 97, 104222.

limits: Nothing in this literature has money on it. Baron, Fetherstonhaugh, Bartels, Mata and Ziano all asked for ratings, rankings, choices or hypothetical allocations, and no participant's answer moved a real budget. The samples are narrow at the origin. Bartels ran all four studies on Northwestern undergraduates, Fetherstonhaugh used Oregon students and one undergraduate class, and Mata's first study used 100 psychology undergraduates. The effect also depends on how the question is put, by the original authors' own account. Fetherstonhaugh got 65% proportion-driven answers when diseases were presented one per page and 16% when the three were laid out together, and attributed the gap to ease of comparison. Bartels found the opposite pattern in his own Study 1, where the individual-differences correlation appeared in joint evaluation but not in separate evaluation, r(43) = .050, p = .746, which he reads as the two being dissociable effects. Ziano's extensions found no moderation by geographic closeness of the target country, and none by political ideology, familiarity with refugee crises or preference for domestic over foreign aid. This entry located no meta-analysis of proportion dominance. Crossref and web searches for pooled quantitative synthesis returned nothing, and the largest body of evidence remains Ziano's five collections. Where the effect comes from is also unsettled: Fetherstonhaugh's group favour a psychophysical value function, Baron argues in the same volume for a general confusion of proportions with differences, and Mata's data point to a failure of deliberation rather than a taste for proportions.
misreadings: Proportion dominance is not the identifiable victim effect, though it is often offered as an explanation of it. The two make different predictions and have different evidence behind them, and this atlas records the pooled identifiable victim effect as near zero. Second, the direction is not fixed. Ziano's three replications of the refugee-camp study found people preferring the larger camp, which is the opposite of numbing, so the pattern is not a law about denominators. Third, Baron's experiment is sometimes cited as showing that proportion beats number. It shows both mattering, with the number of lives saved carrying the larger effect, $143 against $74, than the ratio did, $129 against $89. Fourth, Bartels's 48% is a share of item responses on one half of a rating scale, not a count of people who chose to save fewer lives. Finally, Fetherstonhaugh's paper does not agree with itself on its own headline number. The results section and Table 3 give 65% of respondents, n = 107, showing numbing in Task 1; the discussion says over 67%. The method reports 165 respondents and the Task 2 table reports 164.
